verses.translation_literal: A psalm. Sing to YHWH a song new, for wonders he has done; has saved for him his right hand, and the arm of his holiness.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm. Sing to the LORD — and let it be a song no one has sung before, for what he has done is past all wonder. No army stood beside him. His own right hand won the day, and his holy arm, bared and outstretched, finished it.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open with a shout, not a hymn. The whole psalm is a summons to a crowd, and the verb 'sing' is a plural command: this is a congregation being called to its feet. 'A new song' is not a request for fresh melodies; in the Psalter it is the song that answers a new act of God, and here the act is a victory.

The last line is the one the translations soften. Hebrew says the right hand 'saved for him' (hoshi'ah lo): God's own arm does the saving and the deliverance is his, with no human ally. The KJV's 'hath gotten him the victory' makes it a prize he gains; the ASV 'wrought salvation for him' and YLT are closer; BBE's 'has overcome' drops the word 'salvation' entirely, and with it the echo of yeshu'ah in the next two verses. The 'holy arm' is a warrior image: the bared arm that strikes, as in the language of the Exodus. Note that the Hebrew verse begins with the superscription 'mizmor', which the KJV numbers as verse 0.

philological_notes.note: A 'new song' answers a fresh act of God, and the phrase recurs at the head of Pss 96, 98 and 149. The newness is the occasion, not the tune.

'Has saved'. It shares its root with yeshu'ah in verses 2 and 3, so the psalm's refrain of salvation begins here. Metzudat David reads it as 'he needs no help from another, for his right hand saved for him'.
'The arm of his holiness': a holy arm is the arm set apart for God's own acts. Ibn Ezra notes it is stretched out and reaches the place of his desire.

verses.translation_literal: He has made known, YHWH, his salvation; to the eyes of the nations he has uncovered his righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD has made it known: his salvation. Not whispered in a corner, not carried by a runner from one village to the next. He has stripped the covering from his justice in front of the nations, and every eye that looks can see it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The line is built as a pair, and the actors should play it as one thought said twice, the second time louder. "Made known" (הוֹדִיעַ) is the ordinary word for informing; "uncovered" (גִּלָּה) is the verb for stripping off a cloth or lifting a veil, and it is the verb of exile too (the same root as גולה). The second half raises the first: what was news is now an unveiling. Radak reads it just so: "the last half of the verse is the explanation of the first half" (Radak on Psalm 98:2). Malbim reads it differently, and the two views are worth giving the cast. For Malbim, salvation (the act) and righteousness (the attribute) are not the same thing: righteousness is what moves God to save, and salvation is what it produces. Salvation had to arrive, righteousness was always there and only had to be revealed. Metzudat David adds that the salvation had been announced by the prophets before it came, and now the proof is public.

The stage is "the eyes of the nations" (לְעֵינֵי הַגּוֹיִם), and the KJV's "in the sight of the heathen" is the one loaded word to check. Hebrew גּוֹיִם is simply "nations", every people other than the speaker's own, with no contempt in it; "heathen" brings in a later Christian sense of the unbaptized. The KJV also turns the Hebrew's order (verb, subject, object, then the audience) into "his righteousness hath he openly shewed", and the adverb "openly" is its own gloss for the idea in לְעֵינֵי. BBE blurs the picture further with "given to all the knowledge of his salvation", which loses the visual image: this is a public viewing, not instruction. In ancient Near Eastern terms, a god's victory was displayed in front of rival peoples, and the audience is the point.

philological_notes.note: To uncover, strip, reveal; the root also gives גּוֹלָה, 'exile'. Here it is the unveiling of something that was always present and hidden. Malbim contrasts it with salvation, which has to arrive, whereas righteousness only has to be revealed.

'His righteousness' in the Psalms often stands for God's saving, vindicating action, so that the word sits next to 'salvation' as near-synonym or as cause. Radak takes the two halves as one idea explained twice; Malbim takes righteousness as the motive and salvation as the deed.

verses.translation_literal: He has remembered his covenant-loyalty and his faithfulness to the house of Israel; they have seen, all the ends of the earth, the salvation of our God.
verses.translation_dramatic: He remembered. Through all the long silence he had not forgotten his loyal love, nor the faithful word he gave to the house of Israel. And now the farthest edges of the earth have seen it: the salvation of our God.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Remember' in Hebrew is an act, not a memory: when God remembers, he moves. This is the turn of the psalm, from the broad world to the particular family. Hesed (covenant loyalty) and 'emunah (faithfulness) are the two words that carry God's promise to Israel; the KJV's 'mercy' and 'truth' are the older English pair, and 'mercy' softens hesed, which is a duty of loyalty and not mere pity. The ASV's 'lovingkindness' is closer. Radak reads the faithfulness as God's pledge to bring Israel out of exile; Metzudat David as the kindness he promised.

The verb 'they have seen' lands with a wide camera: 'all the ends of the earth' are the world's far boundaries, and the final phrase moves from 'his' to 'our God'. The singer includes himself in the family: the world watches Israel's God, and the congregation answers, 'ours'.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, the steadfast love that binds God to his promise; neither 'mercy' (KJV) nor mere kindness. Meiri glosses the pair as 'his promise'.
'The ends of the earth': the limits where land stops. Metzudat David reads it as those who dwell at the earth's edges.

verses.translation_literal: Shout, to YHWH, all the earth; break out and ring out and make music.
verses.translation_dramatic: Shout! Shout to the LORD, all the earth. Let the mouths fly open and the sound come pouring out, a cry, then a ringing song, then music, one breaking on the next like waves.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four imperatives in a row, and no one has been asked to be polite. הָרִיעוּ is a shout, the sound of a battle cry or of a crowd greeting its king; the KJV's "make a joyful noise" is a lovely phrase, but it makes the sound sound like an amateur choir. Ibn Ezra's gloss is plain: "to make the voice heard" (Ibn Ezra on Psalm 98:4), and he says the same of the following two verbs. The cast should not sing yet. This is the roar when a monarch steps out.

Malbim gives the stage direction: the custom is that while the king is shut in his palace the people sing songs and psalms to the lyre, but when he comes out and shows himself to the people, they all raise a great shout, the sign that their king is among them (Malbim on Psalm 98:4). That fits the order here: shout first, then "break out" and sing. פִּצְחוּ is literally to split or open (the mouth), and Metzudat Zion links it to Isaiah 52:9, "break forth, sing together"; Radak glosses it "open a song". The KJV's "make a loud noise" for פִּצְחוּ turns an image of a mouth bursting open into volume. The whole earth is summoned, not Israel alone, and Radak says even the nations should rejoice because the salvation brings an end to war between peoples (Radak on Psalm 98:4). The KJV's "unto the Lord" is accurate for לַיהוָה, but "before" would be nearer in the next verse, where the shout is made to a king.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of רוע: to raise a shout, the war-cry or the acclamation of a king, a loud and public sound. In the next verses it is set 'before the king', which makes the royal sense plain.
To split open, break out; used with 'sing' for a song that bursts out. Metzudat Zion links it to Isaiah 52:9 and glosses it as 'open the mouth'.

verses.translation_literal: Make music to YHWH with a lyre, with a lyre, and the sound of music.
verses.translation_dramatic: Make music for the LORD. Strike the lyre, the lyre alone, and then the lyre with a voice rising above it, the sound of song.
verses.directors_commentary:
The doubled 'with a lyre' is deliberate: it is the sound of the instrument struck once, then struck again under a singer. Ibn Ezra and Radak read the repetition as two stages: first the lyre by itself, then the lyre together with the voice of song. Hear the pause between them.

The kinnor was the small hand-held lyre, the instrument of David and of the Levitical singers; it is not a modern harp, which the KJV's 'harp' suggests. BBE's 'instruments of music' blurs it into something generic. The phrase 'voice of zimrah' is literally the 'sound of music' and the KJV 'voice of a psalm' gives the noun a title the word does not carry.

philological_notes.note: The small lyre, held in the arm and plucked; the instrument of David. 'Harp' in the KJV misleads a modern ear.
The repeated 'with a lyre' is read by Ibn Ezra and Radak as the lyre alone, then the lyre with the voice of song.

verses.translation_literal: With trumpets and the sound of the ram's horn, shout before the king, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Now the metal and the horn. Trumpets, and the long cry of the ram's horn, and under it all the roar of a people shouting before the king, the LORD himself.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes from the string to the brass, and with it from the private to the public. The chatsotserah was a straight metal trumpet, blown by priests; the shofar is the twisted ram's horn. They are never the same instrument, and the KJV's 'cornet' for shofar is an old English horn that misleads, since the Hebrew word is the ram's horn blown at coronations and festivals.

The last two words, 'the king, YHWH', are the point. Ibn Ezra says the word 'king' is added because this is how those who go out to meet him at his coming behave: this is the sound of a royal arrival, and the psalm has now named whose. The verb is again hari'u, the same shout as in verse 4. Radak places the scene at the temple: the people come to shout before him there.

philological_notes.note: Straight metal trumpets, blown by priests in temple and in war (Num 10). Metzudat Zion defines the word simply as the name of an instrument.
The ram's horn, blown for assemblies, coronations and alarms. 'Cornet' (KJV) is a misleading translation.

verses.translation_literal: Let it thunder, the sea and its fullness, the world and those dwelling in it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the sea thunder, and everything it holds. Let the whole inhabited world answer it, and every living soul within.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera pulls back from the temple to the whole creation. The sea in the ancient Near East was not scenery; it was the chaos the gods fought, and in Canaanite myth Yam was a rival of Baal. Here the sea is not an enemy to be defeated but a voice in the choir: it thunders for the LORD. That is quiet polemic against the stories of the neighbors.

The KJV's 'roar' is acceptable, but the Hebrew verb is ra'am, 'to thunder', the sound of storm and of a sea slamming a coast. 'The fulness thereof' is 'what fills it', its creatures. Tevel is the inhabited world, as opposed to the dry land generally. Metzudat David hears actual thunder in joy; Radak and Meiri take the whole as figure, and Ibn Ezra adds that sailors and others will rejoice.

philological_notes.note: 'Let it thunder': the verb of thunder, used here of the sea's roar. Metzudat David: 'a thunder sound is heard for joy'.
The inhabited, fertile world, the world of people; Malbim separates it from 'eretz' as the place where human beings live.

verses.translation_literal: Rivers, let them clap palm; together mountains, let them sing for joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the rivers clap their hands. And let the mountains, all together, break into song.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture is deliberately absurd and delightful: rivers with palms, mountains with throats. Rashi says the prophets spoke in language the ear hears, not that rivers have palms, but a word of joy and gladness. Radak and Metzudat David say plainly: it is figure, like clapping at a coronation (2 Kings 11:12).

The KJV's 'floods' for neharot is heavier than the Hebrew, which is simply 'rivers', and the singular 'palm' (kaf, not 'hands') is in the text: the rivers clap palm to palm, as a crowd does at an enthronement. Yimcha'u is the verb of striking one palm on another. And 'together' (yachad) is a single word that binds the choir: rivers in the valleys, mountains above, all at once. Notice how the order runs from the lowest and moving to the highest and still.

philological_notes.note: 'Let them clap the palm': the same gesture of enthronement as in 2 Kings 11:12. Metzudat Zion links it to Ezek 25:6.
'Together': holds all the mountains in one chorus, as Metzudat David says.

verses.translation_literal: Before YHWH, for he is coming to judge the earth; he will judge [the] world with righteousness, and peoples with uprightnesses.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let it all be done before the LORD, for he is coming, coming to judge the earth. And when he judges, he will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples with a level hand, with straight measure for every one of them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The whole chorus of sea, rivers and mountains has been rejoicing, and here the Psalm tells us why: a judge is on the road. For us "judgment" is a threat; for the ancient audience it is the good news. A king or god who "judges" (שָׁפַט) sets right: he rescues the wronged and puts the oppressor down. Radak puts it so, that the verdict will be good for the righteous and evil for the wicked (Radak on Psalm 98:9), and Metzudat David adds that the joy takes place "before the LORD" because he is coming to judge (Metzudat David on Psalm 98:9). Note the grammar: the coming is announced (בָא), and then the judging is in the future (יִשְׁפֹּט), so the actors should play a long pause between arrival at the gate and the verdict.

The word בָא can be read two ways. As a perfect it is "has come", which is how STEPBible tags it and how YLT and BBE render it; as a participle it is "is coming", the reading of the KJV and ASV ("cometh"). The two have different stagings: one is the king already in the square, the other is the king at the horizon. This translation takes the participle, because the verse pairs it with a future judgment and leaves the arrival still ahead; the Targum's אֲתָא looks like a perfect, so the other reading has real support. The KJV's "the people with equity" is accurate in sense but "equity" is a legal term from a different system. The Hebrew מֵישָׁרִים is a plural, "evennesses" or "straightnesses": a level road, a fair scale. Metzudat David glosses it: "just judgment, as is proper for each and every one". The double pairing (earth and world, righteousness and uprightness) is the closing flourish of the Psalm.

philological_notes.note: A form that is read either as the perfect, 'has come' (so STEPBible's tagging, YLT, BBE), or as the participle, 'is coming' (KJV, ASV). The translation chooses the participle, since the verse sets it against the future 'he will judge'. The Targum has אֲתָא, which reads as a perfect, so this is a judgment call, and the staging differs: arrival under way, or arrival complete.

A plural abstract from ישר, 'straight, level': evenness, uprightness. It describes a judgment that treats each party on the same level. Metzudat David glosses it as just judgment, fitting for each and every person.
